prompt: This lesson unzips Gradle into `~/opt` and never adds it to `PATH`. Why is that enough?
hint: Count how many times the lesson types the full path.

choices.text: Gradle stops working when it is found through PATH, so it has to be called by its full path
choices.why: Gradle runs the same from PATH as from a full path; leaving it off PATH is a choice about how often you need it.

choices.text: A command on PATH would hide `mvn`, and the two tools cannot both be on it
choices.why: Two programs with different names live on PATH side by side; `gradle` and `mvn` never collide.

choices.text: It is used once, to generate the wrapper, and every later build runs `./gradlew`
choices.why: Right. The project's wrapper fetches and runs its own Gradle, so the copy in `~/opt` only has to start that once.

choices.text: A change to PATH needs the computer restarted before it takes effect
choices.why: A new PATH takes effect in a new shell, or at once with `export`; no restart is involved, and that is not the reason here anyway.

prompt: `sha256sum` printed the same 64 characters that services.gradle.org publishes for 9.8.1. What does that match establish?
hint: A checksum compares two copies of the same bytes.

choices.text: That the zip will run on the JDK 25 installed on this machine as well
choices.why: A checksum says nothing about compatibility; `gradle --version` running is what showed that.

choices.text: That the zip on disk is byte for byte the one Gradle published
choices.why: Right. A redirect, a mirror or a broken download would each give a different sum.

choices.text: That 9.8.1 is the newest Gradle release
choices.why: Every release has its own checksum, old or new; a match only ties this file to the version you asked for.

choices.text: That services.gradle.org itself can never be tampered with
choices.why: Both the zip and the sum came from Gradle's servers, so a check like this cannot vouch for those servers; it vouches for the transfer.

prompt: Match each piece of lesson 1's pom to the line of the Gradle build that says the same thing.
hint: One line on the right has no counterpart in the pom.

prompt: A colleague copies this lesson's `build.gradle.kts` and deletes the `repositories` block, reasoning that Central is the default anyway. What happens on the next build?
hint: Compare what Maven and Gradle each assume when nothing is said.

choices.text: It builds as before, because Gradle falls back to Maven Central the way Maven does
choices.why: That is Maven's behaviour. Gradle declares no repository unless the build names one.

choices.text: Resolving the dependencies fails, because Gradle has nowhere to look for them
choices.why: Right. With no repository declared, Gradle cannot find commons-validator or JUnit and says so.

choices.text: Gradle reads the jars from `~/.m2/repository`, which lesson 1 already filled
choices.why: Gradle keeps its own cache under `~/.gradle/caches` and only reads a Maven local repository when the build names `mavenLocal()`.

choices.text: It builds, fetching everything from the Gradle Plugin Portal instead
choices.why: The plugin portal serves plugins to the `plugins` block; ordinary dependencies need a repository named in `repositories`.

prompt: In `build.gradle.kts`, a library that the main code compiles against and needs at run time is declared inside `dependencies` with the configuration `___`.
What does `plugins { application }` add to this build? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of these is what lesson 23 does for the bookshop with another tool.

choices.text: Everything the `java` plugin brings: compiling, testing and the jar
choices.why: Right. `application` applies `java` first and builds on it.

choices.text: A `run` task that starts `mainClass` with the dependencies on the classpath
choices.why: Right. That is how `./gradlew run --args=...` worked without anybody typing a classpath.

choices.text: Launcher scripts and a distribution zip with the dependencies beside the jar
choices.why: Right. `startScripts`, `distZip` and `distTar` are the plugin's, and the archive carries a `lib/` directory.

choices.text: A single jar with commons-validator unpacked inside it, runnable with `java -jar`
choices.why: The jar still holds only the project's own classes. A jar with its dependencies inside is a different technique; lesson 23 builds Spring Boot's.

prompt: Which files that `gradle wrapper` wrote belong in the repository, so that a colleague can clone it and build?
hint: A colleague who has never installed Gradle has to be able to type `./gradlew build`.

choices.text: `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` alone; the scripts are generated again on each machine
choices.why: Nothing regenerates them: a fresh clone without `gradlew` has no command to type.

choices.text: `gradlew` and `gradlew.bat` alone; the jar is downloaded on first use
choices.why: The scripts start `gradle-wrapper.jar`, which is what does the downloading; without it they have nothing to run.

choices.text: `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat`, and both files under `gradle/wrapper/`
choices.why: Right. Scripts, the small jar they start, and the properties that name the version and its checksum: all four are committed.

choices.text: None of them: each developer runs `gradle wrapper` after cloning
choices.why: That needs Gradle installed on every machine, at a version nobody controls, which is what the wrapper exists to avoid.

prompt: A colleague has an older Gradle 8 installed system-wide and runs `./gradlew build` in this project. Which Gradle runs the build?
hint: Read `distributionUrl`.

choices.text: Gradle 8, because an installed Gradle always takes precedence over a download
choices.why: `./gradlew` never looks for an installed Gradle; it reads the properties file and nothing else.

choices.text: Gradle 9.8.1, downloaded once into `~/.gradle/wrapper/dists` and reused afterwards
choices.why: Right. The version is the project's, written in `gradle-wrapper.properties`, whatever the machine has installed.

choices.text: Neither: the wrapper stops and asks which one to use
choices.why: The wrapper asks nothing; the answer is already in the properties file.

choices.text: Gradle 8, after it rewrites `gradle-wrapper.properties` to match itself
choices.why: Only running the `wrapper` task changes that file, and an installed Gradle is never consulted by `./gradlew`.

prompt: A proxy at a colleague's company serves a different file at the `distributionUrl` address. With `distributionSha256Sum` in `gradle-wrapper.properties`, what does `./gradlew` do?
hint: The sum was written into the file by the command that generated the wrapper.

choices.text: It prints a warning and builds with the file it received
choices.why: A checksum that only warned would be a checksum anybody could ignore; the wrapper treats a mismatch as fatal.

choices.text: It downloads the file again until the sum matches
choices.why: The same address through the same proxy gives the same wrong bytes; the wrapper does not loop.

choices.text: It builds, because `validateDistributionUrl=true` already proved the address is genuine
choices.why: That setting checks that the URL answers before writing it into the file; it says nothing about the bytes served later.

choices.text: It refuses the file and stops
choices.why: Right. That refusal is what writing the sum into a committed file buys: every machine checks the download the same way.

prompt: Put in order what happens the first time `./gradlew build` runs on a machine that has never seen this project.
hint: The script can only start what is in the repository.
items: `gradlew` starts `gradle-wrapper.jar` with the JDK it finds
The zip is downloaded and its SHA-256 compared with `distributionSha256Sum`
A daemon of that Gradle starts and runs the build
trap: Unpacking before checking the sum would run code from a file nobody has verified.

prompt: Which tasks does `./gradlew run` execute in this project?
hint: Follow the arrows into `run` in the graph, and no further.

choices.text: `compileJava`, `classes` and `run`
choices.why: Right. `run` needs the compiled classes and their classpath, nothing more; `processResources` is in the chain too, with nothing to do.

choices.text: Every task of `build`, and then `run`
choices.why: That is Maven's picture, where a later phase includes every earlier one. Gradle runs only what `run` depends on.

choices.text: `compileJava`, `compileTestJava`, `test` and `run`, so that untested code is never started
choices.why: Nothing in the graph links `run` to the tests, as the transcript shows: no test task appears in it.

choices.text: `jar` and `run`, because `run` starts the jar
choices.why: `run` puts `build/classes` on the classpath directly; no jar is made for it.

prompt: In lesson 1, `mvn package` ran the tests before making the jar. What does `./gradlew jar` do with the tests?
hint: Maven's phases form a line; Gradle's tasks form a graph.

choices.text: It runs them first, because a jar must never be built from untested code
choices.why: That is what Maven's lifecycle enforces by position. In Gradle, `jar` depends on `classes` and on nothing about tests.

choices.text: It compiles them but does not run them
choices.why: `compileTestJava` is on the test branch of the graph, which `jar` never reaches.

choices.text: Neither: `jar` needs only the main classes
choices.why: Right. To make a jar only after the tests pass, ask for `build`, which needs both `assemble` and `check`.

choices.text: It runs them only if a test file changed since the last build
choices.why: Change detection decides whether a task in the graph runs again; it never adds a task the request did not need.

prompt: After deleting the launcher line, `./gradlew test` failed with "Failed to load JUnit Platform". Which tasks had already succeeded by then?
hint: The failure is about starting the tests, not about compiling them.

choices.text: None: Gradle checks every dependency before running any task
choices.why: Gradle resolves a configuration when a task needs it; the test runtime classpath was only needed by `test` itself.

choices.text: Only `compileJava`; the test classes need the launcher to compile
choices.why: No test class mentions the launcher, so the test sources compile without it.

choices.text: All of `build` except `test`
choices.why: `./gradlew test` never asked for `jar` or the distributions; they are not in that request's graph.

choices.text: The compile tasks for both the main and the test code
choices.why: Right. Both compiled; only starting the tests needed the launcher, so `test` was the first task to fail.

prompt: Match each task to what it leaves under `build/`.
hint: The `ls` after the first build shows two of them.

prompt: The second `./gradlew build` in a row printed `UP-TO-DATE` beside every task. What did Gradle compare to decide that?
hint: It is the same comparison for every task.

choices.text: The time of the last build against the clock
choices.why: Time passing changes nothing about a task's inputs, and an idle hour does not make a build stale.

choices.text: Each task's inputs and outputs, against the last run
choices.why: Right. Same sources, same classpath, same settings and the outputs still in place: there is nothing to do.

choices.text: The Git commit of the project against the previous build's commit
choices.why: Gradle knows nothing about Git here; it fingerprints files, which works in a directory that is not a repository at all.

choices.text: The modification times of the source files against those of the class files
choices.why: That is the stale-source check Maven's compiler plugin makes. The `touch` that follows in this section shows Gradle does not.

prompt: After `touch src/main/java/com/example/isbn/IsbnCheck.java`, every task stayed `UP-TO-DATE`. What would lesson 1's `mvn package` most likely have done after the same `touch`?
hint: Maven's compiler plugin decides staleness by comparing two dates.

choices.text: Compiled the class again, because the source is now newer than its class file
choices.why: Right. A newer timestamp is a stale source to Maven's compiler plugin, while Gradle hashes the contents and sees no change.

choices.text: Nothing, because Maven also compares file contents
choices.why: Maven's compiler plugin compares timestamps; that is exactly the difference this demonstration isolates.

choices.text: Failed, because a touched file counts as a corrupted file
choices.why: A new modification time is an ordinary event to every build tool; nothing treats it as damage.

choices.text: Deleted `target/` and rebuilt everything from scratch
choices.why: Only `mvn clean` deletes `target/`; a changed timestamp makes the compiler recompile, it does not clean.

prompt: Changing the separator printed by `main` re-ran `compileJava` and `test`, yet `compileTestJava` stayed `UP-TO-DATE`. Why the difference between the two test tasks?
hint: One task reads the test sources against the main code's signatures; the other runs the main code.

choices.text: Gradle skips compiling tests whenever they passed on the previous run
choices.why: A passing result has nothing to do with it: edit a test file and `compileTestJava` runs whether or not the tests passed before.

choices.text: Test compilation reads the main class's signatures; running tests reads its bytecode
choices.why: Right. This is compile avoidance: a change inside a method body cannot break code compiled against the class, but it can change what a test observes.

choices.text: `compileTestJava` only looks at `src/test`, so a change in `src/main` can never affect it
choices.why: Add a public method to `IsbnCheck` and `compileTestJava` runs again: the main classes are one of its inputs, compared by their signatures.

choices.text: The configuration cache kept the test classes from the earlier build
choices.why: The configuration cache stores the task graph, not any task's output, and it was not even switched on at that point.

prompt: In the second `./gradlew clean build` with the build cache on, how many tasks came `FROM-CACHE`?
hint: Read the summary line under `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`.

prompt: After `clean`, the second build still took `compileJava` `FROM-CACHE`, where `UP-TO-DATE` was no longer possible. What tells the two apart?
hint: Think about where the outputs were when the build started.

choices.text: Whether the outputs were still in `build/` or copied from the cache
choices.why: Right. `clean` removed `build/`, so nothing was up to date, but the cache under `~/.gradle/caches` still held outputs for the same inputs.

choices.text: `FROM-CACHE` is reported when the task ran faster than usual
choices.why: The labels are not timings; each names where the outputs came from.

choices.text: `UP-TO-DATE` reuses outputs from another machine; `FROM-CACHE` reuses them from this one
choices.why: It is closer to the reverse: up to date is always local, and a build cache can be shared, as a remote cache on a server.

choices.text: They are two names for the same outcome, chosen by the console mode
choices.why: Delete `build/` and only the cache can help; the two outcomes need different things to be true.

prompt: Two dependencies ask for different versions of the same library, one directly and one deeper in the tree. Which rule does each tool apply by default?
hint: This lesson's dependency report showed Gradle's rule as an arrow.

choices.text: Both take the highest version requested
choices.why: That is Gradle's rule only. Maven picks by position in the tree.

choices.text: Maven takes the declaration nearest the project; Gradle takes the highest version
choices.why: Right. Here the two happened to agree on commons-logging 1.4.0, for different reasons; on another tree they can disagree.

choices.text: Maven takes the highest version; Gradle takes the declaration nearest the project
choices.why: The other way round: `1.3.5 -> 1.4.0` was Gradle raising a deeper request to the highest one.

choices.text: Both stop the build and ask for the conflict to be resolved by hand
choices.why: Neither fails by default; both choose silently, which is why reading the tree matters.

prompt: Why does this course build the bookshop with Maven from lesson 4 onwards?
hint: The section says what the choice is about, and what it is not about.

choices.text: Spring Boot cannot be built with Gradle
choices.why: Spring Boot ships a Gradle plugin, and its own source code builds with Gradle.

choices.text: Gradle cannot run JUnit tests without extra plugins
choices.why: This lesson ran JUnit 6 tests with Gradle using nothing beyond the `java` plugin and the launcher.

choices.text: A pom is one declarative file, read top to bottom
choices.why: Right. Every lesson that changes the build shows one block of it changing, and nothing taught later depends on the choice.

choices.text: Maven builds are faster on large projects
choices.why: If anything the model favours Gradle on large projects; speed is not the reason given.

prompt: A CI server builds every pull request from a fresh clone, in a new container each time. Which of Gradle's mechanisms can save it from compiling code that has not changed?
hint: Ask which mechanism needs a previous `build/` directory to be there.

choices.text: Up-to-date checks, because the inputs are the same as on the last run
choices.why: An up-to-date check compares against what is in `build/` on this machine, and a fresh clone has no `build/` at all.

choices.text: The configuration cache, because it stores the compiled classes
choices.why: The configuration cache stores the task graph; it never holds a task's outputs.

choices.text: The daemon, because it keeps the classes in memory between builds
choices.why: A new container starts a new daemon, and a daemon keeps a warm JVM, not the project's outputs.

choices.text: A build cache shared by the CI machines
choices.why: Right. A shared, remote build cache is the one mechanism that works across clean checkouts and machines.

prompt: A teammate writes a task that renders a version banner from a template file and from the current Git commit, but declares only the template as an input. After a new commit, `./gradlew build` reports the task `UP-TO-DATE` and the banner shows the old commit. Why?
hint: Gradle can only compare what it was told about.

choices.text: Gradle never re-runs a custom task, only the ones plugins provide
choices.why: Custom tasks get exactly the same checks; the check is only as complete as the inputs declared.

choices.text: The commit is an undeclared input, so the fingerprint did not change when it did
choices.why: Right. An input Gradle does not know about cannot make a task stale; declaring the commit as an input fixes it.

choices.text: The daemon cached the old commit in memory and must be stopped
choices.why: Stopping the daemon changes nothing: the next build compares the same declared inputs and finds them equal.

choices.text: Up-to-date checks only look at timestamps, and the template file was not touched
choices.why: Gradle compares contents, not times; the trouble is which contents it was told to compare.

prompt: Which of these changes make `compileTestJava` run again on the next build? Choose all that apply.
hint: Its inputs are the test sources, the test compile classpath, and the main classes' signatures.

choices.text: Adding a public method to `IsbnCheck`
choices.why: Right. A new public method changes the class's signatures, which is what the test compilation is compared against.

choices.text: Editing `IsbnCheckTest.java`
choices.why: Right. The test sources are its own input.

choices.text: Raising `junit-jupiter` from 6.0.3 to a later version
choices.why: Right. A different jar on the test compile classpath is a different input.

choices.text: Changing the text `main` prints between an ISBN and its verdict
choices.why: That changes a method body and no signature, which this lesson's transcript showed: `compileTestJava` stayed `UP-TO-DATE`.

choices.text: Running `touch` on `IsbnCheck.java`
choices.why: A new timestamp with the same contents is no change at all to Gradle.

prompt: Put these tasks in an order `./gradlew build` can run them in.
hint: Each task comes after everything it needs.
trap: `compileTestJava` cannot come before `classes`: the tests are compiled against the main classes.
